questions.prompt: What is \(GL_n(\mathbb R)\)?
questions.answer: It is the general linear group of invertible \(n\times n\) matrices with real entries. Equivalently, \(GL_n(\mathbb R)=\{A\in M_n(\mathbb R):\det A\ne0\}\).

questions.prompt: What is the identity element in a matrix group under multiplication?
questions.answer: The identity element is the identity matrix \(I\). It satisfies \(IA=A\) and \(AI=A\) for every compatible square matrix \(A\).

questions.prompt: What determinant condition tells you a square matrix is in \(GL_n(\mathbb R)\)?
questions.answer: The determinant must be non-zero. A square real matrix \(A\) is in \(GL_n(\mathbb R)\) exactly when \(\det A\ne0\).

questions.prompt: Is a \(2\times3\) real matrix an element of \(GL_2(\mathbb R)\)?
questions.answer: No. Elements of \(GL_2(\mathbb R)\) must be invertible \(2\times2\) matrices. A \(2\times3\) matrix is not square, so it is not in \(GL_2(\mathbb R)\).

questions.prompt: Determine whether \(\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&2\end{pmatrix}\) is in \(GL_2(\mathbb R)\).
questions.answer: Its determinant is \((1)(2)-(0)(0)=2\). Since \(2\ne0\), the matrix is invertible and lies in \(GL_2(\mathbb R)\).

questions.prompt: Determine whether \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\) is in \(GL_2(\mathbb R)\).
questions.answer: The determinant is \((1)(4)-(2)(2)=4-4=0\). Since the determinant is zero, the matrix is not invertible and is not in \(GL_2(\mathbb R)\).

questions.prompt: For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&0\\0&3\end{pmatrix}\), find \(A^{-1}\).
questions.answer: A diagonal matrix is inverted by inverting its non-zero diagonal entries. Thus \(A^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}1/2&0\\0&1/3\end{pmatrix}\). Multiplying gives the identity matrix.

questions.prompt: Why is matrix multiplication generally not commutative?
questions.answer: For matrices, the row-column products depend on order. It is possible for \(AB\) and \(BA\) to both be defined but have different entries. Therefore matrix groups need not be abelian.

questions.prompt: Compute the determinant of the rotation matrix \(R(\theta)=\begin{pmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta\\\sin\theta&\cos\theta\end{pmatrix}\).
questions.answer: Use the \(2\times2\) formula: \(\det R=(\cos\theta)(\cos\theta)-(-\sin\theta)(\sin\theta)\). This is \(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1\). Therefore every such rotation matrix is invertible.

questions.prompt: Show that the product of two invertible matrices is invertible by giving its inverse.
questions.answer: If \(A\) and \(B\) are invertible, then \((AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}\). Check: \((AB)(B^{-1}A^{-1})=A(BB^{-1})A^{-1}=AIA^{-1}=I\), and similarly on the other side.

questions.prompt: Verify that \(\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) is in \(GL_2(\mathbb R)\) and interpret it geometrically.
questions.answer: The determinant is \((0)(0)-(-1)(1)=1\), so it is invertible and belongs to \(GL_2(\mathbb R)\). Geometrically, it is rotation by \(90^\circ\) in the plane.

questions.prompt: Give an example of two invertible \(2\times2\) matrices \(A,B\) with \(AB\ne BA\).
questions.answer: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(B=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\). Then \(AB=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}\), while \(BA=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\). They differ, and both matrices have determinant \(1\), so both are invertible.

questions.prompt: Verify the group axioms for \(GL_n(\mathbb R)\) under multiplication.
questions.answer: Closure holds because the product of invertible matrices is invertible. Associativity is inherited from matrix multiplication. The identity matrix \(I\) is invertible and acts as identity. If \(A\in GL_n(\mathbb R)\), then \(A^{-1}\) exists and is also invertible. Hence \(GL_n(\mathbb R)\) is a group.

questions.prompt: Show that the set of \(2\times2\) real matrices with determinant \(1\) is closed under multiplication.
questions.answer: Let \(A\) and \(B\) have determinant \(1\). The determinant product rule gives \(\det(AB)=\det(A)\det(B)=1\cdot1=1\). Therefore \(AB\) also has determinant \(1\), so the set is closed under multiplication.

questions.prompt: Show that a \(2\times2\) matrix with determinant \(1\) has an inverse that also has determinant \(1\).
questions.answer: If \(A\) has determinant \(1\), then \(AA^{-1}=I\). Taking determinants gives \(\det(A)\det(A^{-1})=\det(I)=1\). Since \(\det(A)=1\), it follows that \(\det(A^{-1})=1\).

questions.prompt: Explain why all real \(2\times2\) matrices do not form a group under multiplication.
questions.answer: The set contains singular matrices, such as \(\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{pmatrix}\), whose determinant is \(0\). Such matrices have no inverse. Since a group requires every element to have an inverse in the set, all \(2\times2\) matrices do not form a group under multiplication.

questions.prompt: For \(A=\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\), compute \(A^n\) for positive integers \(n\).
questions.answer: Multiplying shows \(A^2=\begin{pmatrix}1&4\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\) and \(A^3=\begin{pmatrix}1&6\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\). The pattern is \(A^n=\begin{pmatrix}1&2n\\0&1\end{pmatrix}\). This can be proved by induction using one more multiplication by \(A\).

questions.prompt: A student says \(A^{-1}\) is found by taking the reciprocal of every entry of \(A\). Diagnose the error.
questions.answer: A matrix inverse is defined by \(AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I\), not by entrywise reciprocals. Entrywise reciprocals often do not even make sense when entries are zero, and they generally do not produce a matrix product equal to \(I\). One must use determinant and adjugate methods or row reduction.

questions.prompt: Prove that if \(A\in GL_n(\mathbb R)\), then \(A^{-1}\in GL_n(\mathbb R)\).
questions.answer: Since \(A\in GL_n(\mathbb R)\), there is a matrix \(A^{-1}\) with \(AA^{-1}=A^{-1}A=I\). The inverse of \(A^{-1}\) is \(A\), so \(A^{-1}\) is itself invertible. It is also an \(n\times n\) real matrix, hence \(A^{-1}\in GL_n(\mathbb R)\).

questions.prompt: Explain why rotation matrices form a subgroup of \(GL_2(\mathbb R)\).
questions.answer: Each rotation matrix has determinant \(1\), so it lies in \(GL_2(\mathbb R)\). The product of rotations through angles \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) is rotation through \(\alpha+\beta\), so closure holds. The identity is rotation through \(0\). The inverse of rotation through \(\theta\) is rotation through \(-\theta\). Thus the rotation matrices form a subgroup.
